evidence_quotes.quote: They capped the cisterns and wells that pumped the water up from the aquifers and distributed it to the communities. In its place, they built a pipe system to distribute treated river water.

The activist narrative analyzed here allows a glimpse of the debacle that accompanied the 1990s privatization of the Buenos Aires water and sewage utility and its return to state control after Argentina’s economic crisis of 2001.
But AA came in, put in piped water and made paying for it obligatory whether we wanted it or not, whether we used it or not.

On July 31, 2007, I interviewed Lic. María Inéz Nagy, the hydro-geologist in charge of subterranean potable water in AySA’s Buenos Aires planning office. Nagy confirmed Cassal’s basic assessment of the cause of water problems in Almirante Brown.
And as the water started to spread through the sewage and fluvial drainage system, 60-65 percent of all the people began to have septic problems.

criterion_notes.c1: Although the first two narratives examine shipping-channel sedimentation/dredging and historical destruction of indigenous agricultural terraces rather than household WASH services, the third substantive empirical section ('Perils of Privatization: The Neighborhood of Almirante Brown, Matanza-Riachuelo Basin', pp. 216-218) directly examines community and household potable water supply (capping of community aquifer wells/cisterns and replacement with piped treated river water) and household sanitation (septic system functioning).
criterion_notes.c2: Both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 are satisfied via the Almirante Brown case, though the paper as a whole is somewhat borderline because its overarching frame is ecological/hydrological balance and its first two narratives concern macro-level waterway and watershed governance. Under the plain wording, the study clearly examines water governance, hydropolitics, maritime/environmental law, and utility privatization/renationalization. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the third empirical narrative examines specific institutional and regulatory mechanisms directly governing household water service: (1) utility ownership and service-delivery restructuring under privatized Aguas Argentinas (AA) and renationalized AySA, which capped decentralized community wells and mandated connection to centralized piped river water; (2) compulsory billing/tariff and cost-recovery rules ('made paying for it obligatory whether we wanted it or not, whether we used it or not', water price hikes, and refusal to reopen wells because the utility needed a return on prior pipe-network investments); and (3) legal potability requirements and the lack of institutional certification procedures preventing reopening of neighborhood aquifer pumps.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative ethnographic study drawing on 2007 fieldwork in Greater Buenos Aires, including interviews with an Almirante Brown resident/water activist (April 3, 2007), AySA's hydrogeologist in charge of subterranean potable water (July 31, 2007), AySA's plant operations chief (April 2007), a maritime lawyer (March 29, 2007), and a geographer (May 22, 2007), alongside participant observation and documentary analysis. Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal/ethnographic empirical studies are eligible regardless of lack of quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: In the Almirante Brown case, the paper reports qualitative and informant-estimated outcomes relevant to source access, compulsory connection, affordability, and sanitation reliability: loss of access to free community/household aquifer wells, obligatory billing and water price hikes for piped river water, rising groundwater flooding homes/streets, and widespread household sanitation failure (informant-reported 60-65% of residents experiencing waterlogged septic problems).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (households and neighborhoods in the conurban district of Almirante Brown, Greater Buenos Aires, studied via key-informant interviews and ethnography), exposure (utility privatization/renationalization, mandatory capping of community wells, obligatory piped-water billing/cost recovery, and potability-regulation constraints), outcome (loss of free well access, compulsory payment/price hikes for piped water, groundwater flooding, and septic system failures), and qualitative ethnographic case-study design are all identifiable.

study_design: Qualitative ethnographic multi-case study (key-informant interviews, participant observation, and documentary analysis)
country: Argentina (with regional waterway context extending into Paraguay and Brazil)
population_and_sample: Households and neighborhoods in the conurban district (partido) of Almirante Brown in Greater Buenos Aires, Argentina (within a multi-sited 2007 ethnographic study interviewing 5 named/pseudonymous key informants including a neighborhood water activist and utility officials, plus participant observation).
exposure: Privatization of the Buenos Aires water and sewage utility (Aguas Argentinas) and subsequent renationalization (AySA), specifically utility capping of community/household aquifer wells, mandatory transition and obligatory billing/cost-recovery rules for piped treated river water, and legal potability-testing institutional barriers keeping community wells shut.
outcome: Elimination of access to free community/household aquifer water, compulsory payment and price hikes for piped river water, rising groundwater flooding homes and streets, and widespread household sanitation disruption (waterlogged septic systems affecting a reported 60-65% of residents).
rationale: Included (with medium confidence) based on the paper's third primary ethnographic case ('Perils of Privatization: The Neighborhood of Almirante Brown, Matanza-Riachuelo Basin', pp. 216-218). While the first two narratives address river shipping-channel dredging and historical plantation destruction of indigenous agricultural terraces (which alone would be out of scope), the Almirante Brown narrative uses primary 2007 interviews with a neighborhood resident/activist and an AySA hydrogeologist to examine how utility privatization (Aguas Argentinas) and renationalization (AySA) governed household potable water and sanitation. Specifically, it analyzes rule-type mechanisms under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 readings—utility ownership/restructuring that capped decentralized community wells, obligatory billing and cost-recovery imperatives for piped river water regardless of household preference or use, and legal potability-certification gaps blocking well reopening—and documents resulting impacts on source access, affordability (price hikes and mandatory payment replacing free well water), and household sanitation reliability (septic system failures alongside groundwater flooding).
